ascii-table.quickAnswer: ASCII assigns every common character a number from 0 to 127. For example, the capital letter A is 65, lowercase a is 97, and the digit 0 is 48. Type any character above to see its code instantly, or type a code to see its character.
keyFacts: ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) defines 128 characters, numbered 0 to 127.
Codes 0-31 are control characters (like TAB = 9, LF = 10, ESC = 27) that do not print.
Code 32 is Space; 48-57 are digits 0-9; 65-90 are A-Z; 97-122 are a-z.
Uppercase and lowercase letters differ by exactly 32 (A=65, a=97).
Modern text is usually UTF-8, which is backward-compatible: the first 128 UTF-8 codes are identical to ASCII.
howTo: Use the search box to filter by code number, character, or name (try "65", "A", or "line").
Type a character in the first box to see its ASCII code.
Type a code (0-127) in the second box to see its character.
Tap the copy button on any row to copy a printable character.
ascii-table.formula:
No formula - ASCII is a fixed lookup table.
Handy relationships: lowercase = uppercase + 32.
Digit character value = code − 48 (so "7" is 55, and 55 − 48 = 7).
ascii-table.workedExample:
Encode the word "Hi":
1. H is uppercase: code 72.
2. i is lowercase: code 105.
3. So "Hi" = 72, 105.
Decode 74 97 117 114:
1. 74 = J, 97 = a, 117 = u, 114 = r.
2. Together: "Jaur".
benefits: All 128 codes on one page - faster than scrolling through long reference sites.
Two-way lookup: character to code and code to character in the same view.
Copy buttons grab symbols without fiddling with keyboard codes.
Useful for programmers debugging text encodings and protocols.
limitations: Covers standard 7-bit ASCII (0-127) only - no extended ASCII or Unicode symbols.
Control characters have no printable symbol, so their copy buttons are hidden.
Names shown are the common short names, not the full formal descriptions.

faqs.q: What is the ASCII code for A?
faqs.a: Capital A is 65. Lowercase a is 97. The whole uppercase alphabet runs 65-90 and lowercase runs 97-122.
Code 32 is the Space character - the blank space you type with the spacebar. It is the first printable character in the table.

Codes 0-31 (plus 127) are control characters. They do not represent printable symbols; they control devices or text flow. Common ones: 9 = horizontal tab, 10 = line feed (new line), 13 = carriage return, 27 = escape.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ASCII and Unicode?
faqs.a: ASCII covers 128 characters - enough for basic English. Unicode covers over 149,000 characters from every writing system. UTF-8, the dominant Unicode encoding, keeps the first 128 codes identical to ASCII, so plain English text looks the same in both.

faqs.q: How do I convert a character to ASCII in code?
faqs.a: In most languages there is a built-in function: Python uses ord("A") which returns 65; JavaScript uses "A".charCodeAt(0); C casts with (int)"A". The reverse uses chr(65) or String.fromCharCode(65).

faqs.q: Why is there a gap between uppercase and lowercase letters?
faqs.a: The 32-code gap (A=65, a=97) was a deliberate design choice in the 1960s so that flipping a single bit (bit 5) converts case. Programmers still exploit this trick today.

mistakes: Codes 0–31 are control characters — they don't print. Copying code 9 (TAB) or 10 (line feed) into a document just moves the cursor.
ASCII stops at 127. Looking up accented letters or currency symbols here won't work — those need Unicode/UTF-8, not this table.
Uppercase A is 65 and lowercase a is 97 — a gap of exactly 32. That's why 'Z' (90) sorts before 'a' (97), so 'Apple' comes before 'apple' in code.
The digit '0' is code 48, not 0. Subtracting '0' (48) from a digit character gives its numeric value — '7' (55) minus 48 = 7.
Code 32 is a real space character, not 'nothing'. Trimming or ignoring it breaks fixed-width text parsing.
